newsitem.title: CROATIA: FEATURE - U.N. hosts Serb, Croat reunions in no-man's land.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - U.N. hosts Serb, Croat reunions in no-man's land.
newsitem.dateline: NO MAN'S LAND, near Osijek, Croatia 1996-09-26

text.p: A U.N. police officer stood on the jagged edge of a destroyed bridge and looked at the thousands milling in the drizzle on the shell-scarred road below.
"This must be just about the happiest place in all of the bits that used to be Yugoslavia," he said, shaking his head in amazement.

The intersection on the main highway that runs between the Croatian towns of Osijek and Vukovar used to be one of the grimmest -- the front line where rebel Serbs and Croat forces struggled for control of the Eastern Slavonia district.
Ringed by mine-fields, it now lies in a belt of No Man's Land that separates the two sides after the local Serb militia prevailed with the help of the Yugoslav National Army (JNA).

Although the fight for Eastern Slavonia was one of the most savage of the battles that shattered the former Yugoslavia, the old front line is now the site of a weekly reunion for thousands of Croats and Serbs who have shelved old animosities.
"Germany, France and other countries (that fought in World War Two) could not stay enemies for ever," said 62-year-old Croat Petar Gradecak. "Neither can we."

"As the situation becomes better, new friendships are being made. You must live," he said as a clutch of relatives from both sides of the ethnic divide gathered round him, trading news and gossip from the past five years.

Like so many families that lived in Eastern Slavonia, the Gradecaks are a mixture of Serb and Croat. Petar's Serb son-in-law now lives in Vukovar with a family of four -- including a four-year-old grandson he had never previously seen.
Petar's face creased with emotion as he embraced the confused youngster for the first time.
Huddled under umbrellas in the drizzle, it was far from an ideal site for a family reunion, but the weather hardly mattered.

"I came just to see some cousins of mine who are living in Osijek," said 34-year-old Predrag -- a Serb who used to work in a sugar factory now on the Croat side of the divide. "But then I bumped into Nebojsa here -- one of my best friends from the old days."
The two men laughed as Predrag slapped Nebojsa on the back. "Now that we see each other, it is as if nothing ever happened. I sometimes wonder what the fuss was about," he said.
The "fuss" was about Croatia's decision to split from the Yugoslav republic in 1991 -- a move the Croatian Serbs violently opposed.
The Serbs of Eastern Slavonia joined their ethnic brethren from two other regions in Croatia in an uprising against the declaration of independence.

In one of the earliest and most bitter cases of ethnic cleansing in the former Yugoslavia, the Croatian Serbs, with the support of the JNA, expelled all Croats from the fertile and oil-rich Danube River plain.
To do it, they used heavy artillery to smash the region's once beautiful Austro-Hungarian town of Vukovar to rubble.
The Serbs surrounded themselves with a buffer zone a kilometre (1/2 mile) wide and built what seemed an unbridgeable emotional gulf between themselves and their old Croat neighbours.
To span that gulf and smooth the region's inevitable return to Croatian control, the U.N. interim administration (UNTAES) decided to experiment with reunions.
UNTAES organised the first gathering on the neutral stretch of road in August, when only 200 people turned up. Since then, the crowd at the weekly event has grown to 8,000.

Some come to trade -- a market of sorts has sprung up in the midst of the throng, where Serbs can buy Croatian toys, chocolates and cigarettes, and Croats snap up cheap plastics and clothes from their old enemies.
Others march past the two kilometre (one mile) long queue of parked cars to get to the meeting point just to mingle, soak up the atmosphere and bump into old friends and neighbours.
"This all goes to show that this conflict was a war of the politicians, and not of the people," beamed a delighted UNTAES spokesman, Philip Arnold.
"You have to be optimistic when you look around a place like this with 8,000 people seeing eath other, kissing, having coffee and so on."
He argued that 8,000 out of a regional population of between 150,000 and 200,000 indicated that the market was not just a fringe phenomenon.

"Just as the smallest number of people committed war crimes, so the smallest number of people are unreconciled to living together again," he said. "I think this market indicates there is considerable hope for a peaceful reintegration."
But Petar Gradecak's wife Marija, whose eldest son was killed by Serbs in the fighting, said it would take more than a friendly market to heal the deep wounds.
"I've left my blood here," she said in a broken voice. "The confidence can hardly be restored as it used to be."
"To meet old Serb friends is one thing. To live in the same neighbourhood again...that is something completely different."
